episodes.213156: The season's first rendition of the North American Monsoon high developed over south-central and southwestern NM with increased low-level moisture intruding beneath it. Faster westerly flow along the northern periphery of the high allowed for some convective organization and stronger afternoon thunderstorms. Relatively warm conditions and low humidity also allowed for strong downdrafts to occur yielding severe wind gusts from decaying thunderstorms mainly over western and central NM each day. Several of these dry downbursts produced blowing dust with one particular event resulting in zero visibility in Rio Rancho on the 25th. Storms through central and eastern NM were wetter in nature threatening locally heavy rainfall and flash flooding. Flash flooding was reported in Raton on the 24th, with another report of heavy rains producing a landslide from steep terrain near Jemez Springs along NM Highway 4 on the 26th. Other storms produced various severe wind gusts and hail across portions of northern and central NM each day.
episodes.213187: Several rounds of thunderstorms occurred during the period of June 25th and June 27th as a frontal boundary remained near the area. Some areas received 3-6 inches of rainfall over a short period of time. Thunderstorms produced a few tornadoes on the evening of June 26th.

A few thunderstorms developed in NY and intensified as they crossed the border into VT.  One storm produced dime size hail as well as damaging winds in Rutland county, VT.

episodes.213459: A warm front set up across central Kansas later in the afternoon and eventually, storms began to develop along it. The strongest storms were mainly across southeast Kansas with damaging wind reported in Montgomery and Labette counties; Parsons Airport had a measured wind gust to 86 mph. As the front slowly tracked to the southeast through the evening, storms became more widespread and trained across the same areas. There was a stronger storm within the activity which produced quarter sized hail in Sedgwick County, but the associated heavy rain was the bigger show. The hardest hit area was the Wichita metro and southern Sedgwick into northern Sumner County where a widespread 4 to 7 inches fell, most of it in a 2 to 3 hour period. Flash flooding reports from Wichita and surrounding areas were plentiful with around 112 reports of stalled vehicles in Wichita alone. Homes along the creeks were also threatened and impacted by flood waters. Basement apartments were evacuated in west Wichita. Just after 10:30 PM KAKE News shared reports on social media from the following intersections of flooded roadways: 13th and Maize, 8th and West, 21st and 295th, Custer and Pawnee, 13th and Rock, Pawnee and Seneca, Central and Tyler. The number of flooded intersections only increased through the next several hours as rain continued. Some of the flooding was due to quickly rising creeks, including the Cowskin in west Wichita, which led to additional street and property flooding.
episodes.213693: A QLCS moved quickly across central and southeast Wyoming during the middle afternoon to late afternoon hours. Most strong gusty winds were reported with a few severe hail reports. Thunderstorm wind damage was reported near Cheyenne, including a derailed train with shipping containers near Interstate 25.
episodes.213695: Severe thunderstorms produced isolated and brief strong wind gusts during the late afternoon and evening hours of June 26th in western Nebraska. Flash flooding was also reported near Scottsbluff and Bridgeport Nebraska.
episodes.213814: High pressure over New Mexico helped trigger new storms off the higher terrain. These storms then moved to the south and east into the combined Panhandles. With favorable instability and wind shear, these storms became strong to severe with the main hazards being large hail and damaging winds. There were some supercells that did produce tornadoes across portions of the eastern combined Panhandles as well as high end wind damage from straight line winds. Given sufficient moisture in place, slow moving storms or storms that moved over the same locations, a few communities in the eastern combined Panhandles did receive heavy rainfall that resulted in flash flooding.
episodes.213839: A cold front pulled moist air into the region during the early portions of June 26th.  Morning clouds gave way during the afternoon, which allowed for the atmosphere to become more unstable. Thunderstorms initially developed in northeastern New Mexico and moved into the Panhandles during the evening and overnight of June 26th. As they encountered the moist, unstable air, they strengthened and organized into a fast-moving squall line. Damaging straight line winds were the main threat with these storms. A few storms ahead of the squall line were able to produce large hail but overall the atmosphere was not as conducive for large hail given the potential for melting to occur.
episodes.214098: Very hot temperatures and convergence within a surface trough allowed scattered thunderstorms to develop late in the afternoon on the 25th. The hot temperatures allowed storms to be high based producing mostly severe wind gusts. One of the more robust updrafts produced quarter size hail in the city of Lubbock. The most impressive storm of the evening was one that tracked near Slaton (Lubbock County). This storm generated a microburst with a peak wind gust of 110 mph measured by the Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet. A storm survey the next day revealed very localized damage around the mesonet site northeast of Slaton. Cotton crops were destroyed and mesquite trees were stripped. Additionally, irrigation pivots were damaged and partially rolled. A heavy gate damaged the fence surrounding the mesonet site but no damage to the sensors occurred. Later in the evening, a line of thunderstorms developed on an outflow boundary moving into the northwestern South Plains. These thunderstorms continued to produce intermittent severe wind gusts as they tracked across the northern South Plains into the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle.
episodes.214151: Disturbances in the upper-level flow, coupled with upslope flow in the higher terrain, caused shower and thunderstorm development across west Texas and southeast New Mexico. Dry low-levels allowed several storms to produce strong downbursts, the strongest of which occurred in Seagraves, where damage to multiple buildings was reported.
episodes.214356: Several severe thunderstorms impacted portions of western Oklahoma on the evening and night of the 25th. An initial supercell thunderstorm (previously tornadic across Beaver County, Oklahoma) moved into northwestern Oklahoma and produced hail and severe winds. Additional thunderstorm activity moved eastward off of a dryline across the eastern Texas Panhandle, producing occasional reports of large hail and damaging winds.
episodes.214357: Scattered thunderstorms developed in the vicinity of a weak surface front/pressure trough across northern Oklahoma on the evening of the 26th. This activity produced damaging winds, hail and flooding as it progressed south/southeastward into the early morning of the 27th. Significant damaging winds and hail were noted with a trio of more organized thunderstorms (supercells) during this time impacting areas around Enid, Stillwater, Oklahoma City and Chandler, OK.
episodes.214470: Clusters of strong thunderstorms along the coast produced a few measured wind gusts in excess of 34 knots.

episodes.214820: Weak surface high pressure ridging was centered just to the south of the JAX CWA on both the 26th and 27th, resulting in a west to southwest flow across the region. Sufficient moisture and summertime instability resulted in numerous showers and thunderstorms, with some strong to severe storms causing isolated reports of damage across the area.

episodes.215521: On June 25, 2026, into the early morning of June 26, the NWS Buffalo region transitioned into an unsettled convective pattern as a warm front lifting across the lower Great Lakes was closely followed by a cold front tied to a mid-level trough. According to NWS Buffalo Area Forecast Discussions, early morning low stratus and patchy river valley fog���particularly across the Western Southern Tier���cleared through the day, allowing boundary layer destabilization with 500 to 1,000 J/kg of MUCAPE (and localized pockets up to 1,500 J/kg). The Storm Prediction Center placed the region under a Marginal Risk for severe weather, emphasizing that 30 to 40 knots of 0���6 km bulk shear combined with steepening low-level lapse rates would support multi-cell storm clusters capable of localized damaging wind gusts. Simultaneously, atmospheric precipitable water levels surged toward 1.4 inches, prompting Weather Prediction Center highlights for localized heavy downpours capable of minor urban and small-stream flooding. As the cold front swept eastward Thursday evening and convective intensity waned, cool cyclonic flow over the warm lake waters initiated lake-enhanced rain showers and localized low clouds across Western New York into the early morning of June 26. One very strong thunderstorm developed over Lake Ontario in the early morning hours of June 26, and produced large hail over the eastern shore of Lake Ontario.
episodes.215756: Persistent enhanced westerly flow with multiple embedded shortwave troughs brought multiple instances of severe wind gusts and hail to northern Utah as well as flash flooding to Sevier county.
episodes.215826: On June 26th an approaching cold front associated with an upper level shortwave trough brought strong shear and modest mid level instability to New Hampshire.  Daytime heating was near seasonable norms, but still enough to create amble low level instability as highs reached the lower 80s.  A few long track storms created a swath of hail and wind damage from Sullivan to Rockingham Counties.
episodes.215882: Hot and humid conditions under high pressure led to a typical summertime environment capable of supporting strong pulse-type thunderstorms and dangerous lightning.
episodes.215931: An upper-level disturbance permitted an unsettled weather pattern to remain over South Florida and the nearby waters for a portion of late June 2026.
episodes.215973: Multiple rounds of storms occurred June 26-28th, 2026 resulting in significant flash flooding over southern Indiana and central Kentucky as well as an EF-0 tornado.  Several flash flood warnings were issued over the 2 day period with Considerable Flash Flooding in multiple locations and even Flash Flood Emergencies in some areas. Rainfall totals for the weekend ended up in an area wide 2-4 inches with swaths of 6-10+ inches!!  Unfortunately 3 fatalities were confirmed due to flooding in Madison County, KY, and 1 fatality indirectly related to the flooding occurred on Floyds Fork in Jefferson County, KY.

A combination of a storm survey, eyewitness reports, and radar data indicated that damage from a severe storm across western Wheeler County was caused by a strong rear-flank downdraft on the backside of a powerful supercell. The path of the most significant damage was approximately one mile wide. The most severe damage occurred in an RV park, where 16 unanchored travel trailers were rolled and destroyed. The south end of the trailer park was downstream from open areas, which likely contributed to higher wind speeds and greater damage in that specific section of|the park. One injury was reported, but most residents had either evacuated to a shelter or were not home at the time. An overturned pickup truck at the site was likely pushed over by adjacent rolling trailers. Other damage included snapped power poles, numerous broken large tree limbs, and a few uprooted trees. Several homes and businesses sustained significant roof damage, including metal buildings that were compromised after their overhead doors failed. Most well-constructed or newer|structures sustained only minor damage or remained unscathed. Peak wind speeds are estimated to have been near 100 mph. The swath of this damage was about four miles long and about 1800 yards wide.
